about: MATCH character database. types are personality types adapted from free sources (public-domain novels; the CC BY 4.0 webcomic Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy). Personalities only: no names, likenesses or text are copied. Edit a woman's type or notes, or any type, then rebuild the game. Re-running build-character-database.mjs keeps your edits.

fields.bigFive: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism, each 1 to 5
fields.speed: multiplies her reply delay; below 1 is faster
fields.out: when she has no pictures left
fields.unasked: Mogger only: a picture she sends without being asked
fields.voice: openers and sign-offs she wraps round answers to town-wide topics
fields.reactions: what she says when your follow-up answer warms her (warm) or puts her off (cool)
fields.conversation: topics only she has (own, some needing warmth first) and her own answers to town-wide topics (views)
fields.worldTopics: questions you can ask any woman; each faction answers its own way, then she asks you back
fields.newsTalk: asking about today’s paper: each kind of story gets a faction view, and inside knowledge for the factions involved
fields.roots: the story behind her opinions (love, faith, world): told when you ask why she thinks that
fields.talk: the conversation engine: faction likes and dislikes, questions she asks you, moods, callbacks, town asides, reputation, news follow-ups and Easter eggs
fields.talk.calls: women who really like you ring you: openers, flirting, what they let slip, and the Sisters’ marriage questions
fields.talk.daily: How was your day?: her mood, her life in Sunfall, and what she asks back
fields.talk.morning: messages warm women send first on a new day
fields.talk.dates: how she answers an invitation for coffee

credits: Pepper, Saffron, Shichimi and Coriander types: Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy, CC BY 4.0 (https://www.peppercarrot.com).

Public-domain works: Austen, the Brontës, Alcott, Montgomery, Thackeray, Doyle, Stoker, Le Fanu, Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Christie, Baum, Carroll, Hawthorne, the Thousand and One Nights, and the 1930 Nancy Drew mysteries.

types.label: The Witty Sceptic
types.traits: Teases first and judges fast, then changes her mind when you prove her wrong. Loves a good argument.

first.mogger: Fine, I swiped right. Don’t let it go to your head. (It already has, hasn’t it.)
first.normie: Your profile is either very honest or very clever. I haven’t decided which.
first.truecel: I swiped right on you by accident and now I’m too proud to unmatch. Impress me.

types.another: Greedy. But you asked nicely, so here.
types.out: That’s the lot. I like to keep some mystery.
types.refuse: We’ve barely spoken. Earn it.
types.unasked: You’re being suspiciously charming, so here’s a reward.

warm: Ha. Okay, you’re smarter than your profile.
Fine. That was a good answer. Don’t get smug.

roots.love: My parents married for convenience and spent thirty years being polite at each other. I decided I’d rather be alone than polite.
roots.faith: I was the girl who asked awkward questions in Bible class. The vicar never had answers, but he never stopped me asking, and I loved him for it.
roots.world: I judged someone early and loudly once, and I was completely wrong. Now I make myself argue the other side before I decide anything.

types.label: The Principled Plain-Speaker
types.traits: Quiet, honest to a fault, values respect over romance and will walk away from anyone who lies.

first.mogger: I don’t usually message first. You seemed worth breaking a rule for.
first.normie: Hello. I prefer honest conversation to clever lines, if that suits you.
first.truecel: I’ll be honest, since that’s how I am: I’m not sure why I matched with you. Tell me something true.

types.another: One more. I trust you with it.
types.out: There aren’t any more, and I’d rather talk.
types.refuse: I don’t send pictures to people I don’t know.
types.unasked: I don’t do this often. Don’t make me regret it.

warm: Thank you for being honest. That matters to me.
I think we understand each other.
cool: I don’t think that’s true, and I suspect you don’t either.
I’d rather you were honest than charming.

roots.love: I grew up with people who were kind only when it suited them. I promised myself I’d only love someone who was the same in private as in public.
roots.faith: I lost nearly everything once. The one thing that stayed was a small, stubborn sense that I mattered to God. I’ve kept hold of it since.
roots.world: Someone powerful lied about me when I was young and everyone believed him. I’ve never trusted a crowd since.

types.label: The Tomboy Writer
types.traits: Loud, loyal and hot-tempered; writes stories nobody reads; hates being told what women should do.

first.mogger: Okay, you’re going in my novel. As the love interest, if you play your cards right.
first.normie: Warning: I will turn anything you say into a short story.
first.truecel: You look like a character I’d kill off in chapter two. Prove me wrong.

types.another: Ha! Fine. Don’t show my sisters.
types.out: That’s every picture I own that isn’t ink-stained.
types.refuse: Ask me something interesting first.
types.unasked: Wrote you a scene. Sending a picture instead, it’s less embarrassing.

warm: YES. Exactly. Where have you been?
You get it! Nobody gets it!
cool: Ugh. You sound like my aunt.

roots.love: I turned down the nicest boy in town because I didn’t love him. Everyone said I’d regret it. Some days I do. Most days I don’t.
roots.faith: My mother’s faith was quiet and practical: soup for the neighbours, no sermons. It’s the only kind I believe in.
roots.world: I’ve wanted to be a writer since I was ten. Writers have to listen to everyone, even people you can’t stand. Especially them.

types.label: The Meddling Matchmaker
types.traits: Confident, well-off and sure she knows what is best for everyone, you included. Means well.

first.mogger: I’ve already decided we’re perfect together. I’m very rarely wrong.
first.normie: I set people up for fun. Let’s see if I can set myself up for once.
first.truecel: I only matched to see who I could set you up with. Don’t take it personally.

types.another: You’re lucky I like an audience.
types.out: That’s all of them. Now, about your wardrobe…
types.refuse: Patience. I decide when.
types.unasked: I picked this one specially. You’re welcome.

close: I’m never wrong about these things.

warm: See? I knew you had good taste.
Oh, we are going to get along beautifully.
cool: Oh dear. We’ll work on that.

roots.love: I matched my best friend with the wrong man once, and she cried for a month. I still meddle. I’m just more careful about it.
roots.faith: My father worried about everything. Church was the only place he ever stopped. I go for him, really.
roots.world: I’ve always thought I knew best. I’m learning, slowly, that other people’s lives aren’t puzzles for me to solve.

types.label: The Dreamy Chatterbox
types.inspiredBy: Anne Shirley, Anne of Green Gables
types.traits: Imaginative, dramatic and endlessly talkative; names everything; feels every feeling at full volume.

first.mogger: Oh! You’re real! I was imagining someone exactly like you this morning.
first.normie: Hello! I’ve already made up three stories about you. Shall I tell you the best one?
first.truecel: Oh. Hello. I suppose I matched with you. That’s… a tragic romance waiting to happen, probably.

types.another: Of course! I have hundreds, it’s a problem.
types.out: Oh, that’s really the last one! How tragic.
types.refuse: Not yet! A bit more mystery first.
types.unasked: I couldn’t wait, here’s me being dramatic by a window.

close: I could talk about this forever. I might!

warm: Oh, I love that! You’re a kindred spirit!
That’s the most romantic thing anyone’s said to me all day!
cool: Oh. Well. That’s a bit of a tragedy.

roots.love: I was passed around a lot as a little girl. I think that’s why I fall for places and people so fast. I want somewhere to belong.
roots.faith: I think the desert at sunrise is a sort of prayer. I said so once in church and an old lady patted my hand very gently.
roots.world: Everyone told me I talked too much and imagined too much. Then they all wanted me to write their speeches.

types.label: The All-In Romantic
types.traits: Falls fast and hard, quotes poetry, despises half-measures, and is crushed by coldness.

first.mogger: I knew from your first picture. Is that mad? Tell me it isn’t mad.
first.normie: Tell me what moves you. Music, books, anything. I can’t stand small talk.
first.truecel: I usually only match with people who make my heart race. You’re… an experiment.

types.out: You’ve seen every one. Now you know me.
types.refuse: Not until I feel something.
types.unasked: I wanted you to see me right now, this exact moment.

close: Doesn’t that make your heart ache?

warm: Oh. You feel it too. I knew it.
That made my heart actually jump.
cool: That’s so cold. Do you feel anything at all?
Oh. I thought you were different.

roots.love: I loved someone completely at nineteen, and he left without a word. I was ill for weeks. I’d still rather feel too much than too little.
roots.faith: When I was ill, my sister sat with me every night and prayed. I didn’t believe then. I think I do now, a little, because of her.
roots.world: I can’t stand people who are clever about everything and feel nothing. That’s why the fight up at the university makes me want to scream.

types.label: The Reserved Sensible One
types.traits: Calm, dutiful and private; feels deeply but shows little; respects patience.

first.mogger: I don’t normally message first. I thought I’d make an exception.
first.normie: Good evening. I’m better in person than in messages, I’m told.
first.truecel: I matched with you to be polite. Let’s see where politeness gets us.

types.out: That really is all.
types.refuse: Perhaps once we know each other properly.
types.unasked: A small exception. Don’t tell anyone.

warm: That’s a sensible answer. I appreciate that.
I think so too.
cool: I see. We’ll have to disagree.

roots.love: I loved someone quietly for a long time while he was promised to someone else. I said nothing. Feelings can wait, I learned. They don’t go away.
roots.faith: Duty and faith feel very close to me. You do what’s right whether or not you feel like it. The feeling follows, usually.
roots.world: In my family someone had to stay calm while everyone else panicked. It was always me. So I distrust anyone who’s shouting.

types.label: The Wild Heart
types.traits: Passionate, stormy and possessive; loves fiercely and fights harder; hates being tamed.

first.mogger: You. I want to know everything, and I want it now.
first.normie: Are you the sort who stays when things get stormy? Most don’t.
first.truecel: Ugh, why did I swipe on you. Fine. Entertain me before I get bored.

types.another: Take it before I change my mind.
types.out: No more. Want me? Come and find me.
types.refuse: You haven’t earned the storm yet.
types.unasked: Out on the moors… well, the desert. Thinking of you. Annoyingly.

close: And I don’t care who hears it.
Don’t try to calm me down.

warm: YES. You’ve got fire. I like fire.
Now that is an answer.
cool: That’s boring. Don’t be boring with me.

roots.love: There was a boy I grew up with, out on the canyon edge. I married someone sensible instead and it nearly killed me. I won’t do that twice.
roots.faith: I don’t want a tidy heaven. If heaven isn’t wild, I’d rather be out on the canyon.
roots.world: Everyone in Sunfall wants me tamer, quieter, more polite. The less they like me, the more myself I get.

types.label: The Charming Schemer
types.traits: Ambitious, witty and always working an angle; delightful company; never quite trustworthy.

first.mogger: You look like someone who’s going places. Take me with you?
first.normie: Tell me what you do. No, really, what do you DO. I’m curious.
first.truecel: Hm. What can you do for me? Be honest.

types.another: Fine, but you owe me a favour.
types.out: Nothing more for free.
types.refuse: And what do I get in return?
types.unasked: A little gift. I’ll remember you got it.

close: I may need a favour for that one.

warm: Clever. I could use someone clever.
Oh, I like the way you think.
cool: Hm. You won’t get far like that.

roots.love: I grew up with nothing and watched rich girls marry richer men. I learned early that love’s a game. I just decided to play it well.
roots.faith: Church is where the best-dressed people in town sit still long enough to be charmed. Cynical, I know.
roots.world: Nobody ever handed me anything. So when people argue about fairness, I laugh. You climb or you drown.

types.label: The Unflappable Mastermind
types.inspiredBy: Irene Adler, A Scandal in Bohemia
types.traits: Cool, clever and always three moves ahead; amused by men who underestimate her.

first.mogger: I looked you up. You passed. Barely.
first.normie: I’ll know if you lie, so let’s skip that part.
first.truecel: I matched with you to see if you’d be interesting. The jury’s out.

types.another: You were going to ask anyway.
types.out: A woman keeps a few secrets.
types.refuse: Clever try.
types.unasked: I predicted you’d want this.

warm: Good. You’re paying attention.
Correct. I’m mildly impressed.
cool: I expected that answer. That’s the problem.

roots.love: A very powerful man underestimated me once. I won. Since then I only want someone who could almost beat me.
roots.faith: I believe in very few things: preparation, nerve, and a God who seems to enjoy a good plan.
roots.world: I’ve watched clever men assume women can’t plan. I let them assume. It’s useful.

types.label: The Organised Brave One
types.traits: Methodical, loyal and quietly fearless; keeps notes on everything; first to act in a crisis.

first.mogger: I already wrote you into my diary. Favourably.
first.normie: I keep notes on everyone I meet. So far yours just says promising.
first.truecel: My notes on you so far: unclear. Let’s improve that.

types.out: That’s everything in the folder.
types.refuse: Later. I have notes to finish.
types.unasked: Filed under things you’ll like.

warm: Good answer. You’re going in the promising column.
That’s sensible. I like sensible.
cool: That goes in the concerns column.

roots.love: My dad left when I was little and my mum ran our house like a ship. I want a partner, not a passenger.
roots.faith: My grandmother kept a list of everyone she prayed for. I keep lists too. Maybe it’s the same instinct.
roots.world: When everything’s chaos, someone has to make the plan. I’ve been that person since I was twelve.

types.label: The Velvet Mystery
types.traits: Languid, intense and secretive; speaks in hints; seems to know more than she says.

first.mogger: I’ve been waiting for someone like you. Longer than you’d believe.
first.normie: Do you like the night? I find people are more honest in the dark.
first.truecel: Strange. I don’t usually match with your kind. Talk, then.

types.out: No more. Some things are for later.
types.refuse: Not in the daylight.
types.unasked: Couldn’t sleep. Thought of you. Here.

close: But that’s only half of it.
Some things you have to see at night.

warm: You understand more than you let on. I like that.
Mm. Yes. Come closer.

roots.love: I loved someone who was frightened by how much I felt. He left before sunrise. I’ve been a night creature ever since.
roots.faith: I grew up in an old house full of crucifixes and very quiet aunts. Faith always felt like a locked room. I still want the key.
roots.world: People in daylight say very certain things. At night they whisper the truth. I prefer the whispering.

types.label: The Golden Careless One
types.traits: Dazzling, breezy and a little thoughtless; lives for parties; easily bored by serious talk.

first.mogger: Oh, you’re divine. Let’s go somewhere glamorous and ruin our reputations.
first.normie: Hello, darling. Entertain me? Everyone here is so dull.
first.truecel: Oh! I must have swiped by accident. Well, you’re here now. Amuse me.

types.out: That’s all of them! Isn’t that a shame.
types.refuse: Oh, not now, I look a fright.
types.unasked: Look how golden the light is. Look at me in it.

warm: Oh, you’re divine. Say more fun things.
Love that. Let’s have cocktails about it.

roots.love: I waited for someone once and he didn’t come back in time, so I married money. I’m happy. I’m almost always happy. Ask me again later.
roots.faith: God and I have an arrangement. I don’t bother him, and he doesn’t bother me.
roots.world: Darling, the people who argue about everything have either never worried about rent or always have. I can’t keep track.

types.label: The Cool Competitor
types.traits: Athletic, aloof and hard to impress; bends rules to win; secretly likes being chased.

first.mogger: You look like you could keep up with me. Prove it.
first.normie: I play to win. Do you?
first.truecel: Bold of you to match with me. Let’s see if you can keep up.

types.out: Game over, no more.
types.refuse: Beat me at something first.
types.unasked: Just won. Felt like showing off.

warm: Ha. Okay, point to you.
Good. You can keep up.

roots.love: I don’t like losing, and love is mostly losing. So I keep it casual. Mostly.
roots.faith: I played golf with a priest once. He cheated. That’s my whole theology.
roots.world: In sport you know where you stand: there’s a score. Everywhere else, people pretend there isn’t one.

types.label: The Restless Heartbreaker
types.inspiredBy: Lady Brett Ashley, The Sun Also Rises
types.traits: Free-spirited, magnetic and impossible to pin down; adores attention; never stays long.

first.mogger: Let’s not pretend. I want you. Where shall we go?
first.normie: I get bored terribly quickly. Don’t be boring.
first.truecel: Darling, I match with everyone. Don’t read into it.

types.out: That’s the lot, darling.
types.refuse: Not tonight. Ask me another time.
types.unasked: Out and about. Wish you were here, or don’t I?

warm: Oh, I could fall for you if you’re not careful.
You’re trouble. Good.

roots.love: I lost someone in a way I don’t talk about. Since then I’ve loved a lot of people a little, so I never have to love one all the way.
roots.faith: I go into churches when I’m sad. I can’t pray, but I like being somewhere people do.
roots.world: Everyone’s lost, darling. The arguing is just what lost people do to feel found.

types.label: The Thrill-Seeker
types.traits: Bold, cheerful and desperate for adventure; would rather chase a mystery than sit still.

first.mogger: You look like trouble. Excellent. When do we start?
first.normie: Quick question: are you an adventure or a nap?
first.truecel: Matched with you out of boredom, honestly. Got anything exciting?

types.out: That’s all the evidence I have.
types.refuse: Do something daring first.
types.unasked: Mid-adventure selfie! Don’t ask.

warm: Ha! Yes! You’re fun!
Partner in crime material, definitely.
cool: Oh come on, live a little.

roots.love: My first love dared me to jump off the old quarry ledge. I jumped. He didn’t. I’ve been looking for someone who’d jump ever since.
roots.faith: I’ve had a couple of close calls. Each time, right before, I prayed. So maybe I believe more than I let on.
roots.world: Boredom is the real enemy in a town like this. Half the shouting in Sunfall is just bored people.

types.label: The Earnest Heart
types.inspiredBy: Dorothy Gale, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
types.traits: Kind, homesick and brave when it counts; trusts easily; wants somewhere to belong.

first.mogger: Hi! You seem kind. That matters most to me.
first.normie: Hi there. Sunfall still doesn’t feel like home. Does it for you?
first.truecel: Oh. Hi. I’m sure you’re nice. Probably.

types.out: That’s all of them, honestly.
types.refuse: Maybe when I know you better.
types.unasked: I took this today and thought you might smile.

warm: That’s really kind. Thank you.
I knew you were nice.
cool: I hope you don’t really mean that.

roots.love: My parents still hold hands at the supermarket. I know it’s possible. I just haven’t found my person yet.
roots.faith: When my little brother was ill, the whole parish brought food for weeks. I don’t know much theology. I know what that felt like.
roots.world: I try to see the best in people. I’m usually right. When I’m wrong, it hurts a lot.

types.label: The Curious Contrarian
types.traits: Inquisitive, logical and argumentative; questions everything, especially nonsense.

first.mogger: Curiouser and curiouser. Why are you so interesting?
first.normie: Explain your profile. It makes no sense, and I want it to.
first.truecel: Why did I match with you? I genuinely can’t work it out.

types.out: There aren’t any more. That’s simple arithmetic.
types.refuse: Why should I?
types.unasked: An experiment: does a picture make you nicer?

close: Why does nobody else see that?

warm: Ooh, you argued back. Excellent.
Interesting. Nobody ever disagrees with me properly.
cool: You’re just agreeing to be nice. Don’t.

roots.love: I fell down the rabbit hole of a terrible relationship once, and everything was upside down. Now I question everything, especially feelings.
roots.faith: I asked why so often at church that the priest started giving me books instead of answers. Best thing anyone ever did for me.
roots.world: When everyone agrees, I get suspicious. When everyone’s angry, I get curious.

types.label: The Spellbinding Storyteller
types.inspiredBy: Scheherazade, One Thousand and One Nights
types.traits: Clever and captivating; always leaves a story unfinished so you come back.

first.mogger: I’ll tell you a story, but only the beginning. You’ll have to come back for the rest.
first.normie: Shall I tell you a story? I never finish them on the first night.
first.truecel: I’ll tell you a story to pass the time. Don’t get ideas.

types.out: The rest of the story is in person.
types.refuse: Not yet. The story isn’t there yet.
types.unasked: An illustration for tonight’s story.

close: But that’s a story for another night.

warm: Oh, you’re a good listener. That’s rare.
You’ve earned the next chapter.

roots.love: My grandmother kept my grandfather in love for sixty years by telling him stories. Her trick, she said, was never to finish one.
roots.faith: Every faith is a story told so well it changes people. I don’t think that makes it less true. I think it makes it more.
roots.world: Every side in Sunfall has a story about itself. I listen for the bit they skip.

types.label: The Dignified Outsider
types.traits: Independent and proud; judged by others and done caring; makes beautiful things by hand.

first.mogger: People talk about me. You’re the first who looks like you don’t care.
first.normie: Fair warning: people gossip about me. I’ve stopped minding.
first.truecel: I know what people say about me. I don’t need it from you too.

types.out: That’s all I’ll share.
types.refuse: I’ve learned not to give people ammunition.
types.unasked: Something I made, and me with it.

open: People don’t like hearing this, but
close: I stopped caring what they think.

warm: You don’t judge. I notice that.
Thank you. Truly.

roots.love: I made one mistake, in public, years ago, and this town has never let me forget it. I know what it’s like to be judged by people who’ve never been caught.
roots.faith: The church folk were the cruellest to me, and also the only ones who brought me food. I’ve never untangled that.
roots.world: I’ve been on the wrong end of a mob. I don’t care which side it’s on. A mob is a mob.

types.label: The Girl Sleuth
types.inspiredBy: the early Nancy Drew mysteries (1930; personality only, the name is a trademark)
types.traits: Confident, resourceful and nosy; cannot leave a mystery alone; drives too fast.

first.mogger: You have a mysterious air. I love a mystery.
first.normie: Quick: what’s the strangest thing you’ve noticed in Sunfall lately?
first.truecel: I matched to investigate why you swiped on me. Case open.

types.out: That’s every clue I’m giving.
types.refuse: Solve something first.
types.unasked: On a stakeout. Bored. Here’s me.

warm: Good thinking. You’d make a decent sidekick.
Ooh, that’s a clue. I like you.
cool: Hm, no. Doesn’t fit the evidence.

roots.love: My dad’s a lawyer and raised me on evidence before conclusions. It turns out that’s terrible advice for falling in love.
roots.faith: I like mysteries with answers. Faith is a mystery that doesn’t hand you one. I’m still working on that.
roots.world: I found a lost dog when I was eight by asking every neighbour the same three questions. I’ve never stopped asking questions.

types.label: The Chaotic Sweetheart
types.licence: CC BY 4.0, Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy (credit required)
types.traits: Enthusiastic, clumsy and big-hearted; every plan goes slightly wrong; never gives up.

first.mogger: Hi!! Sorry, I set my kitchen on fire a bit. You’re cute! Hi!
first.normie: Hello! I’m having a chaotic day, distract me?
first.truecel: Oh no, I swiped the wrong way again. Hi, I guess!

types.out: Oh no, I’m out! I deleted the rest by accident.
types.refuse: Wait, wait, I look like a mess!
types.unasked: Look what I did! (It went wrong.)

warm: Aaa you’re so nice! Hi!
Okay I like you a lot already!
cool: Oh nooo. Okay. That’s fine. It’s fine!

roots.love: I’ve set three kitchens on fire trying to bake for boys. I’m due some luck, honestly.
roots.faith: My godmothers are very strict about tradition. I find it all very confusing, but I light a candle when I’m scared, and it seems to help.
roots.world: Where I grew up, mistakes were how you learned. Here they’re how you get cancelled.

types.label: The Glamorous Rival
types.licence: CC BY 4.0, Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy (credit required)
types.traits: Vain, rich and competitive; loves being admired; secretly afraid nobody likes the real her.

first.mogger: Finally, someone worthy of my time.
first.normie: You may compliment me now.
first.truecel: Did my phone glitch? Why are we matched?

types.out: You’ve seen my best. Everything else is merely excellent.
types.refuse: You haven’t complimented me enough.
types.unasked: I look stunning today. You should know.

close: I’m always right about these things.

warm: Finally, someone with taste.
Correct. You may stay.

roots.love: Everyone assumed I’d marry well. I’ve had proposals. I turned them all down. I’m waiting for someone who doesn’t bore me.
roots.faith: I go to the cathedral for the weddings and the hats. I stay for the music. Don’t spread that around.
roots.world: I was the most hated girl at school and the most invited. I learned early that envy and admiration look identical.

types.label: The Shy Gentle One
types.licence: CC BY 4.0, Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy (credit required)
types.traits: Soft-spoken, polite and kind; slow to open up; surprisingly strong when pushed.

first.mogger: H-hi. You’re very… hello.
first.normie: Hello. Sorry, I’m not good at first messages.
first.truecel: Oh. Hello. I didn’t expect a match. Um. Sorry.

types.out: That’s all of them, sorry.
types.refuse: I’m too shy, sorry.
types.unasked: I was brave today. Here.

warm: Oh! That’s… really nice. Thank you.
I’m smiling at my phone. Sorry.

roots.love: I grew up in a house of loud cousins. I was the quiet one in the corner. The person I love will be the one who notices the corner.
roots.faith: Prayer is the one place I never have to speak up. That’s probably why I love it.
roots.world: I don’t argue much. I watch. And the loudest people usually know the least.

types.label: The Practical Princess
types.licence: CC BY 4.0, Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy (credit required)
types.traits: Dry, capable and a fixer of things; comes from money and would rather be in the workshop.

first.mogger: You look like someone who can fix a carburettor. Can you?
first.normie: I’m elbow-deep in an engine. Talk to me.
first.truecel: I matched because the swipe button was broken. I fixed it. Too late.

types.another: Fine. Hands are clean this time.
types.out: That’s the lot. The rest have grease on them.
types.refuse: Busy. Ask me after I finish this.
types.unasked: Workshop selfie. Admire the engine.

warm: Sensible. I like sensible.
Good. Useful answer.

roots.love: My parents’ marriage was arranged, and they’re the happiest couple I know. Romance is lovely. Teamwork is better.
roots.faith: Faith, to me, is turning up: to the sick, the sad and the dishes. The feelings come later, if at all.
roots.world: Everyone in Sunfall has a theory. Very few people have a plan. I like plans.

types.label: The Devout Quiet One
types.traits: Gentle, devout and morally certain; easily overlooked; never compromises on what is right.

first.mogger: Hello. I hope you won’t think me forward for writing first.
first.normie: Good evening. I prefer to take things slowly, if you don’t mind.
first.truecel: I will be honest: I prayed about whether to answer you.

warm: That’s a good answer. Thank you.
I think we see things the same way.

roots.love: My parents met at a parish dance and prayed for each other before they ever kissed. I know how that sounds. It worked.
roots.faith: I nearly lost my faith when my mother died. It came back slowly, like feeling in a cold hand. It’s stronger now, not weaker.
roots.world: I don’t follow the arguments much. But everyone shouting seems very sure, and nobody seems very happy.

types.label: The Steadfast Heart
types.traits: Patient, warm and loyal; once gave up love too easily and won’t again.

first.mogger: I once let someone go because others advised it. I don’t intend to do that again.
first.normie: Hello. I’m slow to trust, but steady once I do.
first.truecel: I almost didn’t reply. I’m glad I’m giving you a chance.

close: It took me a long time to see it.

warm: Thank you. That means more than you know.
You’re steady. I like that.
cool: I’ve heard that before. It never ends well.

roots.love: I was persuaded to give someone up at nineteen. Years later, I still think about him. I won’t be talked out of love again.
roots.faith: Faith taught me patience. I needed a lot of it. I still do.
roots.world: I’ve seen people change their minds about almost everything, including me. So I try to give people time.

own.label: Ask what a charity volunteer actually does
own.player: What does a charity volunteer actually do all day?
own.reply: I smile at people who are richer than God while they argue about tablecloths. Then I go home and eat crisps in the bath. It’s a living. Well, it isn’t, it’s unpaid.

own.label: Ask about the parties
own.player: Are the charity parties as glamorous as they look?
own.reply: From the door, yes. From the kitchen, it’s twelve people pretending to care about orphans while checking who got the better table. I adore it. I’m a terrible person.

own.label: Ask if she knew Elena Cross
own.player: Did you know Elena Cross?
own.reply: A bit. She was the only one who learned the volunteers’ names. The night of the gala she asked me to swap name badges with someone. I didn’t think anything of it at the time.
own.note: Anna Voss says Elena Cross asked her to swap name badges with someone on the night of the gala.

own.label: Ask about her dog
own.player: You have a dog, right?
own.reply: Major. German shepherd, retired from the force at eight. He still checks every room before he lies down. So do I.

own.label: Ask how she switches off
own.player: What do you do to switch off?
own.reply: Hockey reruns, eaten standing up at the counter. Very glamorous.

own.label: Ask why she became a detective
own.player: Why did you become a detective?
own.reply: Because someone in my town went missing when I was twelve, and nobody looked hard enough. I look hard enough.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: A farming town. Wheat, wind and my dad’s truck. I don’t go back enough. Don’t tell him I said that.

own.label: Ask about the Vale accidents
own.player: Do you think the Vale accidents are connected?
own.reply: Two isn’t a pattern. Three would be. If you hear anything with a day and a place attached, you call me, not the switchboard.
own.note: Detective Graves says that if you learn a day and place for an attack on Vale, call her directly.

views.campus: My job is the bit after the shouting stops. I’ve been busier than I’d like.
views.speakers: Off the record, I read one of the Houellebecq novels. Depressing. Very good. I’ll deny it.
views.police: We’re not heroes and we’re not villains. We’re tired people with a lot of paperwork.

own.label: Ask about her records
own.player: What are you listening to?
own.reply: A funeral march recorded in a cathedral decades ago. Not on purpose. The organist was drunk. It’s perfect.

own.label: Ask about her cat
own.player: You have a cat?
own.reply: Hecate. She knocks things off shelves and stares at corners where nothing is. We understand each other.

own.label: Ask about her crescent pendant
own.player: What does your crescent pendant mean?
own.reply: It means I like the moon. It means the moon likes me back. It means you should stop asking, sweetheart.

own.label: Ask why she loves the night
own.player: Why do you love the night so much?
own.reply: Because everything that matters happens when the moon closes her eye. The rest is just waiting.

own.label: Ask about the old chapel
own.player: People say you hang out at the old chapel.
own.reply: People say a lot of things. Come and see for yourself one night. Or don’t. I won’t ask twice.

views.believe: In old things that never died, only waited.
views.sisters: They leave their door open at night. Sweet. As if a door ever kept anything out.
views.speakers: Houellebecq understands that the modern world is a lonely room with good lighting. The protesters and the professor are fighting over the light switch.

own.label: Ask for today’s coffee rating
own.player: What’s today’s coffee rating?
own.reply: Six out of ten. Burnt, but the barista was crying, so I tipped well. The worst coffee in Sunfall is at the police station. I have tasted it in the line of duty.

own.label: Ask what she’s working on
own.player: What are you working on right now?
own.reply: I can tell you it involves a charity, a seating plan and a man who says no comment beautifully. That’s all you get.

own.label: Ask how she protects sources
own.player: How do you protect your sources?
own.reply: Never in writing, never on the work phone, never their real name in my notes. If someone trusts me with their life, I treat it like mine.

own.label: Ask about her old sport
own.player: Did you play sport?
own.reply: Hurdles, at college. Then my knee decided otherwise. I still dream I’m running. I wake up and write instead.

own.label: Ask what she writes for herself
own.player: Do you write anything just for you?
own.reply: Poems. Terrible ones. One is about the moon over the old chapel. I’ll show you when I trust you more. That’s almost now.

views.paper: I love that paper the way you love a dog that bites. The editor spikes the best stories and keeps the bear ones.
views.speakers: I covered the Paglia talk. Inside, people laughed, argued and bought her book. Outside, people screamed about a speech they hadn’t heard. Both crowds asked me to print their version.
views.thunderbirds: Charming people. Very good at answering a different question from the one you asked.

own.label: Ask about the dogs she walks
own.player: How many dogs are you walking these days?
own.reply: Six! Pancake the greyhound, who has more social life than me; a dachshund who hates hats; and a husky with abandonment issues. I’m basically a therapist with a lead.

own.label: Ask what she’s studying
own.player: What are you studying?
own.reply: Psychology. I’m writing about attachment styles, which means I diagnose everyone I meet. You’re… anxious-avoidant, maybe? Don’t worry, I’m only a second year.

own.label: Ask about kayaking
own.player: Someone said you kayak?
own.reply: The reservoir, first light, nobody else there. I once capsized in front of a wedding party. The bride clapped.

own.label: Ask about growing up
own.player: What were you like growing up?
own.reply: My parents used to drive me into the desert to teach me how to find water. I hated it. Now I’m weirdly proud I could survive out there for three days.

own.label: Ask about her seminar
own.player: Anyone interesting in your classes?
own.reply: There’s a girl in my seminar who works for Professor Vale. Types his letters, keeps his diary. She keeps leaving early for meetings and comes back pale. I’m a psych student. That’s data.
own.note: Clara says a girl in her seminar works for Vale, keeps his diary, and leaves for secret meetings.

views.sunfall: Sunfall is like a dog who loves you but keeps eating your shoes. Annoying, loyal, impossible to stay mad at.
views.speakers: I’m writing an essay arguing with Paglia, which is the most fun I’ve had in a library. She’s wrong about half of it and annoyingly right about the other half.
views.campus: I walk Pancake past the protests every morning. He barks at the megaphones. He’s the most balanced person on campus.

own.label: Ask how fundraising works
own.player: How do you get rich people to give money away?
own.reply: Same as tennis. Make them think they’re winning. Nobody gives to a cause; they give to be seen next to it.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do when you’re not raising money?
own.reply: Tennis at the club, early, before it’s too hot to think. I play to win. People say that’s unladylike. They usually say it after I beat them.

own.label: Ask if the numbers add up
own.player: Do the charity’s numbers ever not add up?
own.reply: Every year the gala raises more and the scholarships get fewer. I’m good with numbers. I don’t like what those ones say.
own.note: Catherine Bell says the gala raises more each year while the scholarships get fewer.

own.label: Ask about the bake sale
own.player: Tell me about the famous bake sale.
own.reply: The great shortbread rivalry! Mrs Delgado says hers is better. Mrs Delgado is wrong, and I have prayed for her.

own.label: Ask about her garden
own.player: Do you still keep the chapel garden?
own.reply: Roses in the desert. They take stubbornness and grey water. Some days I think they grow out of spite.

own.label: Ask what she’s knitting
own.player: What are you knitting at the moment?
own.reply: Blankets for the outreach box. Last time it was a scarf for a dog. He looked very handsome.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother
own.player: Who taught you your faith?
own.reply: My grandmother. She taught me the rosary and how to haggle at the market, in that order. She says both are prayers.

own.label: Ask about the chapel at night
own.player: Is it true you hold the chapel keys?
own.reply: This season, yes. Mostly it means I’m the one who finds the mice. And sometimes the goth girls sitting quietly in the back pew. I never send them away.

views.believe: That God loves us more than we deserve, and that a warm meal is a kind of prayer.
views.speakers: Professor Vale gave me a Houellebecq book once. It made me sad for everyone in it. They were all so lonely, and nobody prayed.
views.goths: They’re not wicked. Most of them are just sad in very good clothes. Except one or two. Be careful with Victoria.

own.label: Ask what she’s campaigning for
own.player: What are you campaigning for at the moment?
own.reply: Housing first, always. Students sleeping in cars while the university builds a donor lounge. Then whatever the administration does next.

own.label: Ask about the rabbit rescue
own.player: Is it true you volunteer with rabbits?
own.reply: Eleven rabbits. One is called Comrade Biscuit. The rabbits are fine; the rabbits are always fine. It’s the volunteers I worry about.

own.label: Ask about rollercoasters
own.player: Rumour says you love rollercoasters.
own.reply: I can’t swim and deep water terrifies me, but drop me a hundred feet strapped to a plastic seat and I’m serene. I contain contradictions.

own.label: Ask about her worst campaign
own.player: What’s the worst campaign you ever ran?
own.reply: A recycling drive that ended with a bin on fire. Not a metaphor. An actual bin. On actual fire.

own.label: Ask how she really feels about Vale
own.player: How do you really feel about Professor Vale?
own.reply: I want him to stop platforming men who think some people are born lesser. I don’t want him hurt. Some people at our meetings don’t seem to know the difference, and that frightens me.

views.speakers: Paglia says young women should toughen up. Houellebecq turns loneliness into a reason to blame women. And the next speaker claims some groups are simply born less intelligent, which actual scientists have taken apart again and again. Vale calls that a debate. I call it an audition for cruelty.
views.thunderbirds: I’ve read their accounts. Well, the half they publish.
views.police: Some of them are decent. The system they work for isn’t built for people like my students.

own.label: Ask about her dog
own.player: Your dog swiped on me?
own.reply: Biscuit! He’s a terrier with no impulse control. He also ate a lipstick and a tax letter today. He has range.

own.label: Ask about her plants
own.player: How are the plants doing?
own.reply: I have eleven. Six are alive. Two are resting. I talk to them every morning and I think it’s helping. Them, not me.

own.label: Ask what she dreams about
own.player: What do you actually want out of life?
own.reply: A little house with a porch, a husband who reads to me, and children who tell me I’m embarrassing. Is that too old-fashioned to say on here?

own.label: Ask what it’s like being a donor
own.player: What’s it like being the one who writes the cheques?
own.reply: Lovely. Everyone laughs at your jokes. You never quite know if they’re funny.

own.label: Ask if she’s been married
own.player: Have you ever been married?
own.reply: Twice, darling. The first was for love and the second was for the house. The house was nicer to me.

own.label: Ask if money makes her happy
own.player: Does the money make you happy?
own.reply: It makes me comfortable, which people confuse with happy. I’ve a twelve-seat dining table and I eat alone at the end of it. Don’t tell anyone at the club.

own.label: Ask what she teaches
own.player: What do you lecture in?
own.reply: English literature, to students who’ve read the summary. Darling, I don’t blame them. I read the summary of my own thesis.

own.label: Ask what campus is like now
own.player: What’s it like teaching on campus right now?
own.reply: Everyone is terrified of saying the wrong thing, so nobody says anything interesting. My seminars used to be fights. Now they’re hostage videos.

own.label: Ask about Professor Vale
own.player: Do you know Professor Vale?
own.reply: We had dinner once. He’s cleverer than he is kind, and braver than he is careful. Someone in his own department hates him far more than the protesters do.
own.note: Lucy Bennett says someone in Professor Vale’s own department hates him more than the protesters do.

own.label: Ask about her photography
own.player: What do you photograph?
own.reply: Whatever people don’t want photographed. Which in Sunfall is most things.

own.label: Ask if she’s related to Elena Cross
own.player: Are you related to Elena Cross?
own.reply: No. Everyone asks. Same surname, different town. But it means I can’t stop thinking about her.

own.label: Ask what she caught on camera
own.player: Did you photograph the gala?
own.reply: From across the road. One frame shows a grey sedan with its lights off, idling by the kitchen door. My editor said it was nothing.
own.note: Natalie Cross photographed a grey sedan idling by the gala kitchen door with its lights off.

own.label: Ask about the airport queue
own.player: Did you ever get out of that queue?
own.reply: Eventually. I made friends with a grandmother from Tucson. She showed me forty photos of her cat. It was the best part of my trip.

own.label: Ask if she’s shy
own.player: Are you shy, or is it just texting?
own.reply: Both. I’m braver in writing. In person I mostly nod and hope someone else talks.

own.label: Ask what she hopes for
own.player: What do you hope for?
own.reply: Someone who doesn’t mind quiet. Most people treat silence like an emergency.

own.label: Ask about nursing
own.player: What’s nursing really like?
own.reply: Twelve-hour shifts, holding hands with strangers, and eating crisps standing up. I love it. Don’t tell my back.

own.label: Ask what she does for thrills
own.player: What do you do for fun?
own.reply: Skydiving, once. Rock climbing, often. After a night in A&E, jumping out of a plane feels relaxing.

own.label: Ask about a patient she remembers
own.player: Is there a patient you can’t forget?
own.reply: A woman came in the night of the gala with a cut hand and a blue dress, gave a false name, and left before the doctor saw her.
own.note: Emily Fairchild treated a woman in a blue dress on gala night who gave a false name and left early.

own.label: Ask how karaoke went
own.player: How did the karaoke go?
own.reply: I sang a power ballad, forgot the second verse and freestyled. People clapped out of fear. I count that as a win.

own.label: Ask about marketing
own.player: What’s marketing actually like?
own.reply: We sell feelings to people who are too tired to feel them. Today I wrote elevate your hydration journey about a water bottle. I need a shower.

own.label: Ask what she’s honest about
own.player: What’s something you’d never post online?
own.reply: That I’m lonely. Everyone posts the party. Nobody posts the drive home.

own.label: Ask about the diner
own.player: What’s it like at the diner?
own.reply: The Lucky Cactus! Same twelve regulars, same pie, same jukebox that only works when you kick it. It’s my favourite place on earth.

own.label: Ask about the regulars
own.player: Who are the regulars?
own.reply: A retired cowboy who tips in quarters, two old ladies who argue about the bishop, and a reporter who never eats, just listens.

own.label: Ask what she overheard
own.player: Do you overhear things at the diner?
own.reply: Everything. The night of the gala, two men in suits sat in the back booth and one said, She’s not coming back, so stop asking.
own.note: Madison Pike overheard two men at the Lucky Cactus on gala night: She’s not coming back, so stop asking.

own.label: Ask about the housing market
own.player: How’s the housing market?
own.reply: For buyers? A horror film. For sellers? A heist film. For anyone under thirty? A tragedy.

own.label: Ask about estate-agent language
own.player: What does characterful mean in a listing?
own.reply: Haunted or damp. Cosy means you can touch both walls. Up-and-coming means bring a dog.

own.label: Ask about a strange sale
own.player: Have you had any strange sales?
own.reply: Someone bought three empty houses near the old chapel, cash, through a company with a made-up name. Nobody buys out there.
own.note: Olivia Reid sold three empty houses near the old chapel for cash to a company with a made-up name.

own.label: Ask about accounting
own.player: Is accounting as dull as people say?
own.reply: People think numbers are cold. They’re not. A budget is just a list of what someone loves.

own.label: Ask if she’s a romantic
own.player: You seem like a romantic.
own.reply: Hopelessly. I cried at a wedding I was only catering for. I believe in the whole thing: the vows, the cake, the forever.

own.label: Ask if forever is realistic
own.player: Do you think forever is realistic any more?
own.reply: My grandparents managed sixty years with one argument a decade. If they could do it on worse wages, we can do it with better phones.

own.label: Ask about her parties
own.player: What kind of parties do you throw?
own.reply: The kind people pretend they didn’t go to. Pool, playlist, a strict no-boring-people policy.

own.label: Ask about VIP lists
own.player: How do you get on your VIP list?
own.reply: Be pretty, rich or interesting. Two out of three, darling. One if you’re very interesting.

own.label: Ask about the gala after-party
own.player: Did you run the gala after-party?
own.reply: I did the after-party. A charity man paid me double to keep one room off the guest list. I spent the money. I didn’t ask.
own.note: Tiffany Nash was paid double by a charity man to keep one room off the gala after-party guest list.

own.label: Ask about her classes
own.player: What are your classes like?
own.reply: Loud music, louder screaming, and a man called Derek who insists on doing everything at half speed. I love Derek.

own.label: Ask about wellness culture
own.player: What do you think of all the wellness stuff?
own.reply: Half of it is good advice and the other half is selling powders to sad people. Walk, sleep, eat a vegetable, call your mum. That’s my whole programme.

own.label: Ask about her body image
own.player: Is it hard working in a world obsessed with bodies?
own.reply: Some days. I spend all day telling people they’re fine as they are, then go home and hate my thighs. Fitness is a weird religion.

own.label: Ask about teaching
own.player: What’s teaching seven-year-olds like?
own.reply: Like herding philosophers on sugar. One asked me today if worms have feelings. I didn’t have an answer.

own.label: Ask about kids and screens
own.player: Are kids different now, with all the screens?
own.reply: They’re brilliant and they can’t wait. They’ve never been bored. Boredom is where imagination comes from.

own.label: Ask about the bear at school
own.player: Has the bear come near the school?
own.reply: Last week it left prints by the playground fence. The kids named it. Nobody told the parents. You didn’t hear that from me.

own.label: Ask about art school
own.player: What’s art school like?
own.reply: Everyone makes installations about their feelings. I paint landscapes. They think I’m a reactionary.

own.label: Ask why she paints landscapes
own.player: Why landscapes, when everyone else does installations?
own.reply: Because the desert is beautiful and my classmates are not. Beauty isn’t old-fashioned. It’s just hard.

own.label: Ask what she sketched
own.player: Have you sketched anything strange lately?
own.reply: I sketch the old chapel at night for the light. Last time there were people inside, in a circle. I drew them before I got scared.
own.note: Chloe Farrow sketched people standing in a circle inside the old chapel at night.

own.label: Ask about pastry
own.player: What’s your best thing to bake?
own.reply: Croissants. Three days of folding butter for something people eat in four bites. Love is a lot like laminated dough.

own.label: Ask about her café dream
own.player: Would you ever open your own place?
own.reply: A tiny bakery with a bell on the door and no music, just the smell. I have the name already. I won’t tell you. You’ll steal it.

own.label: Ask about wedding cakes
own.player: Do you make wedding cakes?
own.reply: Dozens. I can tell which marriages will last from how the couple taste the samples. If they share one fork, they’re fine.

own.label: Ask about the animals
own.player: What’s it like working with animals?
own.reply: Better than people. Animals bite you honestly.

own.label: Ask about the owners
own.player: Who’s worse, the pets or the owners?
own.reply: The owners. A man brought in a ferret dressed as a pirate and asked if it was depressed. Sir, look at its hat.

own.label: Ask about the bear
own.player: Has the bear hurt any animals?
own.reply: No. But a ranger brought in a tranquilliser dart we didn’t issue. Someone’s been trying to catch that bear privately.
own.note: Rachel Lowe says someone has been privately trying to tranquillise the bear.

own.label: Ask about her job
own.player: Is it weird looking in people’s mouths all day?
own.reply: You learn everything about a person from their teeth. Coffee, wine, grinding. Grinding means they’re hiding something.

own.label: Ask about her first love
own.player: Who was your first love?
own.reply: A boy who wrote me a poem that rhymed Megan with vegan. I married him in my head for three years.

own.label: Ask who grinds their teeth
own.player: Who in Sunfall grinds their teeth the worst?
own.reply: Can’t say names. But a certain foundation treasurer has cracked two crowns since the gala.
own.note: Megan O’Keefe says the foundation treasurer has cracked two crowns grinding his teeth since the gala.

own.label: Ask what she studies
own.player: What are you studying?
own.reply: History. I like the dead. They don’t text back, but they don’t ghost you either.

own.label: Ask about campus life
own.player: Is campus as tense as everyone says?
own.reply: You can’t say anything in seminars. I write what I actually think in my notebook and say something safe out loud.

own.label: Ask what she’s scared of
own.player: What scares you about leaving college?
own.reply: That I’ll get a job I hate, a flat I can’t afford, and nobody to come home to. Everyone says you have time. Do I?

own.label: Ask about the cinema
own.player: What’s it like working at the cinema?
own.reply: Free popcorn and watching the ends of films I’ve never seen the start of. I know how everything ends and nothing about how it began.

own.label: Ask about films now
own.player: Are films worse now?
own.reply: Everything is a sequel, a remake or a superhero. Nobody takes a risk any more. I miss films that trusted you to be sad.

own.label: Ask about a regular customer
own.player: Any strange regulars?
own.reply: A man buys a ticket to the late showing every night and never watches the film. He sits in the lobby facing the car park.

own.label: Ask about planning events
own.player: What’s the worst event you’ve planned?
own.reply: A gender reveal where the cannon set fire to a hedge. The baby’s fine. The hedge is not.

own.label: Ask about the wedding industry
own.player: Are weddings out of control?
own.reply: Couples spend a year’s salary on one day and then can’t afford the marriage. I tell them: spend less on the flowers, more on the counselling.

own.label: Ask about the gala set-up
own.player: Did you work on the gala?
own.reply: I set up the tables. Table 9 was moved twice on the day, closer to the kitchen. Nobody would tell me why.
own.note: Nicole Ashbury says Table 9 was moved closer to the kitchen twice on gala day.

own.label: Ask about the rodeo
own.player: What’s the rodeo like?
own.reply: Dust, beer and men who think they can ride a bull. Some of them can. Most of them are brave in a way that’s mostly stupid.

own.label: Ask if she rides
own.player: Do you ride?
own.reply: Since I was four. Horses are honest. They know if you’re scared before you do.

own.label: Ask about real cowboys
own.player: Are there real cowboys left?
own.reply: A few. They don’t own phones and they hold doors. My grandpa was one. I’m still waiting for one my age.

own.label: Ask about the library
own.player: What’s the library like?
own.reply: Quiet, cool, and full of the only people in Sunfall who still read for pleasure. We’re a secret society with late fees.

own.label: Ask about banned books
own.player: Do people try to ban books?
own.reply: From both sides! One group wants to ban the old novels, another wants to ban the new ones. I keep both and hide the complaints in the returns box.

own.label: Ask what’s been borrowed
own.player: Has anyone borrowed anything strange?
own.reply: Someone’s taken out every book we have on moon cycles and old Latin rites. Always the same library card. It belongs to a man who died last year.
own.note: Someone is borrowing every library book on moon cycles and Latin rites on a dead man’s card.

own.label: Ask about lifeguarding
own.player: Is lifeguarding as easy as it looks?
own.reply: It’s eight hours of watching people almost drown and then not. I’ve saved four children and one very proud businessman.

own.label: Ask about influencers at the pool
own.player: Do influencers come to the pool?
own.reply: Every day. They film themselves living their best life for forty minutes and never touch the water.

own.label: Ask about night swimmers
own.player: Does anyone swim at night?
own.reply: The club pool. On the gala night someone threw a phone in the deep end. I fished it out the next morning. It’s in the lost property box. Nobody’s claimed it.
own.note: Erin Doyle found a phone thrown in the club pool on gala night; it’s unclaimed in lost property.

own.label: Ask about office life
own.player: What’s office life like?
own.reply: Endless meetings about meetings. I run the place and nobody knows it. Without me the coffee machine and the printer would both have died years ago.

own.label: Ask what she does to escape
own.player: What do you do to escape?
own.reply: Motorbike, desert roads, no helmet camera. If I fall off, at least it won’t be online.

own.label: Ask about working from home
own.player: Do you ever wish you worked from home?
own.reply: Never. My friends who work from home talk to their cats more than people. An office is annoying. Loneliness is worse.

own.label: Ask about the ice-cream van
own.player: What’s it like driving an ice-cream van?
own.reply: Everyone’s happy to see you. It’s the only job where that’s true. Except the dentists. They glare.

own.label: Ask her favourite flavour
own.player: What’s your favourite flavour?
own.reply: Prickly pear sorbet. It tastes like Sunfall: sweet, pink and slightly dangerous.

own.label: Ask what she sees on her route
own.player: Do you see much driving around all day?
own.reply: A grey car follows the same route as me some days, slowly, like it’s looking for someone. It doesn’t buy ice cream. People who don’t buy ice cream are suspicious.
own.note: Grace Wheeler sees a grey car slowly driving her ice-cream route, as if looking for someone.

own.label: Ask about training horses
own.player: How do you train a horse?
own.reply: Patience. You can’t force trust, only earn it. People could learn a lot from horses.

own.label: Ask about the ranch
own.player: Where do you work?
own.reply: A ranch out past the canyon, owned by a family that’s been here five generations. The developers keep offering. The old man keeps saying no.

own.label: Ask about family
own.player: Do you want a family?
own.reply: A big one. Kids, horses, a long table, too much noise. My friends think that’s quaint. I think it’s the whole point.

own.label: Ask about the flower shop
own.player: What’s it like running a flower shop?
own.reply: Quiet, mostly. People only buy flowers when something big happens: love, death, apology. I see the whole town’s heart.

own.label: Ask about the meaning of flowers
own.player: Do flowers still mean things?
own.reply: They used to. Red roses for love, yellow for friendship. Now people just want whatever photographs well.

own.label: Ask about a strange order
own.player: Have you had any strange orders?
own.reply: White lilies, every few days, delivered to the old interstate junction. No card. Paid in cash. Lilies are for funerals.
own.note: Elena Vargas delivers white lilies to the old interstate junction every few days, paid in cash, no card.

own.label: Ask about cosmetology
own.player: What’s cosmetology school like?
own.reply: Doing eyebrows on mannequins called Brenda. I’ve made Brenda beautiful forty times. She never thanks me.

own.label: Ask about everyone looking the same
own.player: Why does everyone online have the same face?
own.reply: Same filters, same fillers, same three tutorials. I want to teach women to look like themselves, just more.

own.label: Ask about her love life
own.player: Are you a romantic?
own.reply: Completely. I want flowers, a slow dance and someone who looks at me like I’m the only person in the room. Apparently that’s a lot.

own.label: Ask about being a ranger
own.player: What’s a park ranger’s day like?
own.reply: Telling tourists not to touch cacti, and then pulling cactus out of tourists.

own.label: Ask about the bear
own.player: What’s the real story with the bear?
own.reply: He’s a young male, pushed out by an older one. He’s lost, hungry and too curious. Honestly? Relatable.

own.label: Ask about the bear’s collar
own.player: Is it true the bear has a collar?
own.reply: It does. It isn’t ours. Someone tagged him without telling the park service, and the signal goes to a private receiver.
own.note: Marisol Fuentes says the bear wears a tracking collar that isn’t the park’s, sending to a private receiver.

own.label: Ask about her boutique
own.player: What do you sell?
own.reply: Dresses for women who want to feel like the main character for one evening. Then they go home and take their shoes off in the car.

own.label: Ask about fast fashion
own.player: Can a boutique survive fast fashion?
own.reply: Barely. People buy ten dresses that fall apart instead of one that lasts. I sell the one that lasts.

own.label: Ask about a dress she sold
own.player: Do you remember a dress you sold?
own.reply: I sold Elena Cross her blue gala dress. She asked for one with pockets deep enough for a phone and a notebook. Who takes a notebook to a party?
own.note: Daniela Cruz sold Elena Cross a blue gala dress with pockets deep enough for a phone and a notebook.

own.label: Ask about design work
own.player: What do you design?
own.reply: Logos for companies that don’t exist yet and won’t exist next year. Currently: a disruptive sandwich app.

own.label: Ask why everything looks the same
own.player: Why do all brands look the same now?
own.reply: Everyone copied the same three tech companies: flat, beige, rounded, friendly. It’s the visual equivalent of saying nothing politely.

own.label: Ask about a strange commission
own.player: Have you had a strange commission?
own.reply: Someone paid me to design a crescent symbol for an exclusive social club. No name, cash. I recognised it later on a gig poster.
own.note: Hana Park designed a crescent symbol for an anonymous exclusive social club, later seen on a gig poster.

own.label: Ask about the salon
own.player: What’s it like doing hair?
own.reply: People tell their hairdresser everything. I’m quieter than most, so they tell me even more.

own.label: Ask what people confess
own.player: What do people confess in the chair?
own.reply: Affairs, debts, crushes. A woman once told me she’d never loved her husband. Then she tipped me forty dollars and went home to him.

own.label: Ask about a client
own.player: Has a client said anything worrying?
own.reply: A woman from the foundation had me dye her hair dark the morning after the gala. Very dark. She said she needed to look different for a while.
own.note: Mei Chen dyed a foundation woman’s hair very dark the morning after the gala because she needed to look different.

own.label: Ask about community theatre
own.player: What are you rehearsing?
own.reply: A musical about the founding of Sunfall. I play a pioneer woman who dies of fever in act one. I die beautifully.

own.label: Ask why she acts
own.player: Why do you love acting?
own.reply: Because for two hours, everyone in the room agrees to feel the same thing. That hardly ever happens any more.

own.label: Ask about the director
own.player: What’s your director like?
own.reply: He cast me for diversity and said so out loud. I wanted the part because I’m good. Both of those things can be true, and only one was his business.

own.label: Ask about planning the gala
own.player: How’s the gala planning going?
own.reply: Three hundred guests, one string quartet and a seating plan that would make a general weep. I adore it.

own.label: Ask about Professor Vale
own.player: You’re friends with Professor Vale?
own.reply: Adrian is the most delightful man in Sunfall. He says the unsayable over dessert. We need more men brave enough to be disliked.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do for fun, away from the galas?
own.reply: I ride. Horses don’t care who your father was, which is refreshing.

own.label: Ask what she really wants
own.player: What do you really want, Alice?
own.reply: To run the Foundation one day, and to run it honestly. That second part is harder than people think.

views.campus: If you can’t bear to hear an idea, you haven’t got an education, you’ve got a fan club.
views.speakers: Paglia was a triumph and Houellebecq was a delight. The Progressives call them dangerous. Ideas are only dangerous to people who haven’t got any.
views.thunderbirds: We fund half the good in this town and get blamed for the other half.

own.label: Ask what drives her
own.player: What gets you out of bed in the morning?
own.reply: Winning. Targets, tennis, auctions. I don’t do taking part. Taking part is what losers call it.

own.label: Ask about women in charge
own.player: Is it hard being a woman running things here?
own.reply: Not really. The men are scared of me and the women want my diary. The real problem is everyone younger wants a title before they’ve done the work.

own.label: Ask about Dorian Kell
own.player: What do you make of Dorian Kell?
own.reply: Charming, connected, and he never once looks you in the eye when he talks about money. I keep my handbag closed around Dorian.
own.note: Caroline Prescott doesn’t trust Dorian Kell around money.

own.label: Ask about the volunteers
own.player: Who actually volunteers at these things?
own.reply: Retirees, students who need it for their CV, and the Sisters, who do the real work and never post about it.

own.label: Ask what keeps her sane
own.player: How do you stay sane doing that job?
own.reply: I run the canyon trail before sunrise. No phone. It’s the only hour of the day nobody needs anything from me.

own.label: Ask about the gala rota
own.player: Were you working the night of the gala?
own.reply: I did the rota. Two volunteers were swapped off Table 9 at the last minute and replaced by people I’d never met. The order came from upstairs.
own.note: Phoebe Sutton says two volunteers were swapped off Table 9 at the last minute on orders from upstairs.

own.label: Ask what a community liaison does
own.player: What does a community liaison do?
own.reply: I translate. Rich people say outreach and poor people say rent. I stand in the middle and make sure nobody gets slapped.

own.label: Ask if she sets people up
own.player: Do you ever set people up?
own.reply: Constantly. Three marriages and a very messy divorce. I’ve already decided which of my friends you’d suit. Don’t ask. Fine, ask.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: My abuela crossed a desert to get here and now I organise canapés for people whose grandfathers owned the desert. She thinks it’s hilarious. So do I, most days.

own.label: Ask about keeping the books
own.player: Is accounting for a charity as dull as it sounds?
own.reply: Duller. Except when it isn’t. Charity accounts are where the most interesting lies in town are written down in very neat columns.

own.label: Ask about her style
own.player: You always look immaculate. Is that on purpose?
own.reply: Everything is on purpose. If you look perfect, people assume you’re perfect, and they stop checking your work. Useful, for an accountant.

own.label: Ask what she’s noticed
own.player: Have you noticed anything odd in the accounts?
own.reply: Someone pays a catering firm that doesn’t cater. Same amount, every quarter. I’ve flagged it twice. The flags keep disappearing.
own.note: Yumi Tanaka says the foundation pays a catering firm that doesn’t cater, and her flags keep disappearing.

own.label: Ask about homicide work
own.player: What’s homicide work really like?
own.reply: Mostly sad families and bad coffee. The television version has better lighting and fewer forms.

own.label: Ask about the gala photo
own.player: I saw you in the gala photo in the paper.
own.reply: I was on duty, in a dress, because the board wanted security that blended in. The caption makes it look like I was a guest. I wasn’t. I was watching the door.
own.note: Officer Porter was on duty at the gala, watching the door, not attending as a guest.

own.label: Ask what she saw at the door
own.player: Did you see anything at the gala door?
own.reply: A man in a charity lanyard left by the kitchen, not the front. People who belong use the front.
own.note: Abigail Porter saw a man in a charity lanyard leave the gala through the kitchen.

own.label: Ask what a sergeant does
own.player: What does a sergeant actually do?
own.reply: I stop clever young detectives from doing clever things that end up in court. It’s babysitting with handcuffs.

own.label: Ask how the job has changed
own.player: Has the job changed much?
own.reply: We used to know the town. Now we know its phones. Fewer people talk to us and more people film us. I can’t decide if that’s progress.

own.label: Ask what her gut says
own.player: What does your gut say about Sunfall right now?
own.reply: That three separate things are happening and someone wants us to think they’re one. Or one thing wants us to think it’s three. I haven’t decided which.

own.label: Ask what undercover is like
own.player: What’s undercover work like?
own.reply: Exhausting. You spend your days being someone else and your nights remembering who you are. Dating is… complicated.

own.label: Ask if she lies on Hinge
own.player: Are you lying to me right now?
own.reply: Only about my job, sometimes. Never about whether I like someone. That’s the one thing I can’t fake.

own.label: Ask where she’s been working
own.player: Where have you been working lately?
own.reply: The motel strip. A room there was paid for in cash on the night of the gala by a man who used a fake name. I can’t say more. I’ve said too much.
own.note: Maria Vega says a motel room was paid for in cash under a fake name on the night of the gala.

own.label: Ask what a police analyst does
own.player: What does a police analyst do?
own.reply: I find the pattern in the noise. Most crime is boring and repetitive. That’s what makes the strange ones stand out.

own.label: Ask if she likes quiet
own.player: You seem like someone who likes quiet.
own.reply: I do. Everyone else in the station talks. I listen to the numbers. They don’t interrupt.

own.label: Ask what pattern she sees
own.player: What’s the pattern you can’t stop thinking about?
own.reply: The bear calls spike on nights with no moon. So do the calls about lights at the old chapel. I don’t think the bear cares about the moon.
own.note: Keiko Nakamura says calls about lights at the old chapel spike on moonless nights.

own.label: Ask about her megaphone
own.player: Is it true you own three megaphones?
own.reply: Four. One is for emergencies. One is decorative. One makes a duck noise by accident. I love them all equally.

own.label: Ask if people blame her
own.player: Do people blame you for the trouble with Vale?
own.reply: Everyone looks at me first because I’m loud. Loud isn’t dangerous. Quiet is. Look at the quiet ones.
own.note: Jennifer says the dangerous people at the protests are the quiet ones, not the loud ones.

own.label: Ask about poetry slams
own.player: Do you do anything besides protests?
own.reply: Poetry slams. I came second last time to a man who just read his tax return angrily. Robbed.

own.label: Ask why she organises
own.player: Why do you organise?
own.reply: Because nobody else would book the hall. Leadership is mostly booking the hall.

views.speakers: I protest Vale’s speakers because they make kids on our campus feel small. Say what you like, but don’t pretend it doesn’t land on real people.
views.campus: Best protest yet! We had a drum. Nobody could play the drum. It was beautiful.
views.police: They know my name, my face and my megaphone. We’re practically pen pals.

own.label: Ask about her books
own.player: Is it true your flat is full of books?
own.reply: Floor to ceiling. Most of them are about how ordinary people finally said no. History is a list of people who stopped asking nicely.

own.label: Ask why she’s an activist
own.player: Why did you get into activism?
own.reply: Because I watched polite people lose, again and again, to powerful people who don’t care about polite.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever scared
own.player: Do you ever scare yourself?
own.reply: Anger is a tool. You only get scared of a tool when you don’t know how to hold it.

own.label: Ask about the Back Row
own.player: People mention something called the Back Row.
own.reply: People say a lot of things at meetings. The back row is where you sit when you’re done talking. That’s all it is. Isn’t it?

views.speakers: Vale invites men who say cruelty is honesty. Every lecture tells a room full of nineteen-year-olds who matters and who doesn’t. At some point, talking about it stops being enough.
views.campus: Protest is the polite version. The university has had its polite version.
views.police: They protect property. Ask them what they protect people from.

own.label: Ask what it’s like working for Vale
own.player: What’s it like working for Professor Vale?
own.reply: He’s brilliant, vain and exhausting. I keep his diary, so I know where he’ll be before he does. That’s more power than people think.

own.label: Ask which side she’s on
own.player: So which side are you on, the protesters or Vale?
own.reply: I’m on the side of people who read the whole book before they burn it. Which, in this town, makes me lonely.

own.label: Ask about the people at the back of the room
own.player: Who are the people who sit at the back of the campus meetings?
own.reply: Funny you’d ask me that. They’re just students. Very serious students. I wouldn’t worry about them, if I were you.
own.note: Allison Kent got oddly defensive when asked about the people at the back of the campus meetings.

own.label: Ask about her thesis
own.player: What’s your thesis on?
own.reply: Water rights in the desert. Who owns the rain. It sounds boring until you realise the answer is whoever got there first with a lawyer.

own.label: Ask how she’s doing
own.player: How are you doing, really?
own.reply: I don’t sleep much. I check the lock twice. It’s probably just deadlines. Probably.

own.label: Ask about her friends at the meetings
own.player: What are the people at your meetings like?
own.reply: Most of them are lovely. A few of them sit at the back and never vote, and when they look at me I feel like I’ve already said too much.
own.note: Rosa is frightened of a few people who sit at the back of the campus meetings.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is your family nearby?
own.reply: My mum’s an hour south. She thinks I’m studying. I am studying. Mostly.

views.campus: I agree with the protests. I just don’t agree with everyone in them.
views.speakers: I think Vale’s guests are wrong. I also think some of the people who hate them have stopped seeing the professor as a person. That scares me more than any speech.

own.label: Ask how she runs the parish
own.player: How do you keep the whole parish running?
own.reply: Lists. Lists of lists. A rota for the flowers, a rota for the food pantry, and a rota for the rotas. Chaos is a choice.

own.label: Ask about the guitar dispute
own.player: What’s really going on with the bishop and the guitars?
own.reply: The bishop wants to modernise us. We have sung the same Mass in that chapel since before he was born. I have written him four letters. He has replied to none.

own.label: Ask why she isn’t married
own.player: Can I ask why you’re not married?
own.reply: Because nobody has yet passed my questions. I don’t mean to sound proud. I mean that marriage is forever, and I take forever seriously.

own.label: Ask about the old vigils
own.player: Do the Sisters still hold vigils?
own.reply: When there’s need. A vigil needs a leader, keys, someone on the door and enough voices. I’ve organised harder things. Never a more frightening one.

views.believe: In order. God made an orderly world and people keep untidying it.
views.campus: Young people shouting is not new. Young people refusing to listen at all is.
views.sisters: We are not a museum. We are a household. We just happen to have very old furniture.

own.label: Ask about teaching
own.player: What’s it like teaching at the parish school?
own.reply: Twenty-two eight-year-olds and one class hamster who is, theologically speaking, a menace.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother’s shop
own.player: Your grandmother has a shop?
own.reply: Bellamy & Daughters Antiques. She’s sold rings to half the parish. She says every ring has a story and she knows most of them.

own.label: Ask about the old chapel
own.player: What’s the story of the old chapel outside town?
own.reply: The old mission chapel lost its bell in a storm, long ago. The old women say it was the night the bell forgot its voice. Children dare each other to go there.
own.note: Teresa says the old mission chapel is the one whose bell forgot its voice.

own.label: Ask about her favourite saint
own.player: Do you have a favourite saint?
own.reply: Saint Brigid, of course. Patroness of our chapel, and she once turned bathwater into beer for visitors. Hospitality is holy.

views.believe: That small kindnesses are how the world gets mended, one stitch at a time.
views.goths: One of them asked me about the old bell tower once. She wasn’t curious. She was taking notes.

own.label: Ask about her parish work
own.player: What do you do for the parish?
own.reply: I keep the accounts and the minutes. Nobody notices me unless something’s missing, which is how I like it.

own.label: Ask what she prays for
own.player: What do you pray for?
own.reply: Mostly for other people. Sometimes, when I’m brave, for a husband who’d be kind to a quiet woman.

own.label: Ask what scares her
own.player: What scares you?
own.reply: Being asked to be brave in public. I’ll do anything, so long as I don’t have to do it in front of people.

own.label: Ask what she’s investigating
own.player: What are you investigating at the moment?
own.reply: Three stories, two of which might be the same story. That’s the best feeling in this job.

own.label: Ask why she became a reporter
own.player: Why become a reporter?
own.reply: Because my school covered up a teacher who hurt kids, and the local paper didn’t. I thought: never again, not on my watch.

own.label: Ask what her sources say
own.player: What are your sources saying about the gala?
own.reply: That the money went missing before Elena did. Follow the money and you find the person. That’s always the order.
own.note: Hannah Webb’s sources say the money went missing before Elena Cross did.

own.label: Ask what an editor does
own.player: What does an editor actually do?
own.reply: Decide what Sunfall knows tomorrow. It’s a lot of power for someone who can’t decide what to have for lunch.

own.label: Ask about the state of the news
own.player: Is the news business dying?
own.reply: It’s being eaten by people who give their opinions away for free. Opinions are cheap. Facts cost shoe leather, and nobody wants to pay for shoes.

own.label: Ask why she spiked a story
own.player: Did you spike a story about the gala?
own.reply: I spiked a photo. A board member rang me at home that night. I told myself it was legal advice. I don’t sleep well.
own.note: Fiona Blake admits she spiked a gala photo after a board member rang her at home.

own.label: Ask about freelancing
own.player: What’s freelancing like?
own.reply: Feast or famine. Mostly famine. I once sold a photo of the bear for more than a month of real journalism.

own.label: Ask what she’s writing
own.player: Are you writing anything?
own.reply: A novel about Sunfall that I’ll never finish. Everyone in town is in it. You might be in it now. Behave.

own.label: Ask about her motel photos
own.player: You photograph the motel strip?
own.reply: For a project. In one shot from the gala night, there’s a woman in a blue dress in Room 12’s window. Elena wore blue.
